name: Muse Spark 1.3
about: How Muse Spark 1.3 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Eight billion humans plus globally distributed compute and energy infrastructure cannot be fully destroyed by 2030 short of physics-defying catastrophe.
reasons.2: Faithful value-preserving succession requires human extinction plus solved alignment and survivor AI, a conjunction absent from current trajectories.
reasons.3: Indifferent superintelligence with autonomous replication infrastructure does not yet exist, and four years allows limited time for extinction plus replacement.
reasons.4: Proliferating open and agentic systems could produce multipolar competition without decisive control. Humans still control compute and energy in 2030, limiting full marginalization.
reasons.5: This requires causally separated regions with different civilizational structures. No off-Earth independent civilization exists on a 2030 timeline.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading and population-scale neural integration remain laboratory-scale with no deployment path to dominance by 2030.
reasons.7: A decisive AI power advantage with humans kept alive is the most plausible loss-of-control outcome by 2030. It still requires a sharp capability overhang and control failure in four years.
reasons.8: Legally and economically empowered AI agents could become a peer power center distinct from humans. Multipolar deployment and agent autonomy make this the most likely transformative-but-balanced structure.
reasons.9: Human governments, labs, and firms set objectives, allocate compute, and gate deployment through evals and access controls. Capability growth continues within delegated autonomy without transfer of ultimate civilizational authority.
reasons.10: No actor possesses civilization-wide enforcement capacity for AI arrangements, and multipolar competition blocks such consolidation by 2030.
reasons.11: Economic and military incentives drive accelerated buildout, and no coalition has demonstrated will or means to verifiably dismantle advanced compute.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI within nine years requires a global catastrophe far beyond historical base rates. Industrial AI depends on human-maintained infrastructure that neither war nor accident erases entirely by 2035.
reasons.2: Human extinction with aligned AI succession requires both extinction and successful value preservation in nine years. No demonstrated trajectory produces aligned successors replacing biology that quickly while preserving values.
reasons.3: Fast misaligned takeover followed by human elimination is the most discussed extinction path. Physical bottlenecks and continued human control of compute and infrastructure keep it unlikely by 2035.
reasons.4: Proliferating autonomous agents could escape effective human oversight into multipolar competition without any singleton. Human legal and physical control of compute and energy still constrains full marginalization by 2035.
reasons.5: Causally separated civilizations require self-sustaining off-Earth or substrate-separated settlements. No such separation will mature by 2035.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading and mass neural integration lack demonstrated scalability to population level. Laboratory progress by 2026 does not support dominance of merged agency by 2035.
reasons.7: Unipolar AGI with decisive strategic advantage could concentrate power and render human oversight nominal within nine years. Competitive pressures and rapid capability gains keep this the main alternative to continued human control.
reasons.8: Economically powerful autonomous AIs with independent resources alongside potent human institutions is a natural intermediate from current trajectories. Legal personhood and property for AIs remain immature, limiting full realization by 2035.
reasons.9: Human institutions retained ultimate deployment authority through prior capability jumps and incentives favor continued control.
reasons.10: Civilization-wide irreversible prevention of structural change needs unprecedented global enforcement or omnipotent enforcer. Great-power rivalry and verification problems block this by 2035.
reasons.11: Competitive incentives between states and firms make deliberate global dismantling of powerful AI capacity implausible. Regulation will constrain but not remove the practical ability to build.

reasons.1: Complete destruction of eight billion humans plus all AI infrastructure by 2040 requires global war or catastrophe of unprecedented scale. Base rates for such dual extinction in a fourteen-year window are near zero.
reasons.2: This state requires human extinction combined with a value-aligned successor persisting alone. That conjunction has no precedent and is implausible within fourteen years.
reasons.3: Indifferent ASI eliminating humanity is the central catastrophic misuse and misalignment pathway in technical forecasts. Fourteen years provides limited time for global deployment, takeover, and complete replacement.
reasons.4: Proliferation of open models and autonomous agents favors fragmented competition without central control. Full human marginalization by 2040 is constrained by energy, hardware, and institutional bottlenecks.
reasons.5: Causally separated regions with different civilizational structures require self-sustaining off-Earth settlements or partitioned superintelligences. No Mars or deep-space infrastructure will reach that independence by 2040.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces and radical augmentation are advancing but face biological, safety, and adoption lags. Dominant identity-continuous integration by 2040 is premature.
reasons.7: Centralized AI systems concentrating economic, military, and epistemic power while keeping humans dependent matches current scaling and platform incentives. Decisive power shift without extinction is achievable within fourteen years.
reasons.8: Legal personhood plus economic agency for AI systems alongside intact human institutions describes a multipolar balance extending from current deployment patterns.
reasons.9: Base rates favor incumbent control over 14 years, and this state includes both sub-transformative AI and controlled highly capable AI.
reasons.10: Civilization-wide enforcement of a fixed arrangement requires unprecedented global coordination and monitoring capacity not yet built and hard to complete by 2040.
reasons.11: Permanent dismantling of compute fabs, data centers, and research capacity requires sustained global agreement against economic and military advantage. Competitive pressures make durable universal abandonment implausible by 2040.

reasons.1: Joint extinction by 2050 requires both global catastrophe and failure of hardened AI infrastructure. No current trajectory makes mutual collapse the structure in place.
reasons.2: Value-preserving succession requires both human extinction and successful alignment preservation. This conjunction is unlikely within 24 years.
reasons.3: Rapid capability gains and race incentives open a misalignment window after AGI. Evaluation regimes, control research and state intervention block full displacement in most trajectories by 2050.
reasons.4: Proliferation of open models and autonomous agents favors multipolar competition without decisive control. Human marginalization in such a scramble is plausible.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires self-sustaining off-Earth or isolated compute civilizations. Physics and launch constraints make this infeasible by 2050.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces and radical augmentation are advancing but remain medical and niche. Dominant identity-level fusion across civilization is too slow for 2050.
reasons.7: Centralized AI control with humans kept alive matches takeover scenarios that preserve labor and stability. Capability trends make decisive AI power plausible by 2050.
reasons.8: Legal personhood and autonomous AI economic agency could create a separate AI power bloc. Multipolar institutions make negotiated power-sharing plausible without dominance.
reasons.9: Historical base rates show states and firms retain control of powerful technologies through ownership and regulation. Delegated autonomy with human ultimate authority remains the default path.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance or global governance could freeze structural change but civilization-wide enforcement is hard to build by 2050. Coordination failures cut against a full singleton.
reasons.11: No major productive technology has been verifiably dismantled globally. Economic and military returns to AI prevent sustained universal abandonment by 2050.

reasons.1: Full civilizational suicide by 2060 requires cascading failures in biotech, nuclear, and AI systems simultaneously. Base rates for total extinction on decadal timescales remain very low.
reasons.2: Aligned successor AI that preserves human values yet allows human extinction is conceptually incoherent. It would require beloved caretakers to fail at their core preservation task.
reasons.3: Misaligned decisive superintelligence by the 2040s could treat humanity as irrelevant infrastructure. Thirty-four years provides enough takeoff attempts for this tail risk to matter.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI proliferation with open weights and agent competition favors no singleton and marginalizes slower human actors. Coordination failures make decisive control hard to establish.
reasons.5: Genuinely causally separated civilizations require self-sustaining off-Earth settlements with divergent regimes. Physics and timelines make this effectively impossible by 2060.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading and radical neural integration face severe neuroscience and safety bottlenecks. Dominant population-level fusion is unlikely within 34 years.
reasons.7: A decisive but non-exterminatory takeover where AIs manage economy and governance while humans are kept comfortable fits both capability incentives and alignment partial-success stories. Historical precedent of domestication favors managed irrelevance over murder.
reasons.8: Rough power parity between distinct humans and AIs reflects institutional checks and mutual dependence. This balance is plausible as a transitional snapshot even if unstable.
reasons.9: Humans have retained control through every prior technological revolution via institutions and incremental adaptation. AI governance, evaluations, and capability bottlenecks extend this default.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and global governance could freeze a specific arrangement in place, as major powers actively seek strategic stability. Achieving truly civilization-wide enforcement by 2060 remains logistically difficult.
reasons.11: Deliberate permanent abandonment of powerful AI contradicts strong military and economic incentives to defect. Historical technology bans have never held globally once capabilities are demonstrated.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI requires stacked catastrophes plus failure of bunkered recovery and robust AI self-maintenance by 2070.
reasons.2: Value-faithful succession without survivors is a narrow path requiring both human extinction and successful preservation of human values.
reasons.3: Indifferent optimization and resource competition remain the canonical extinction pathway under fast capability gains with imperfect alignment.
reasons.4: Open proliferation and competitive deployment favor many uncoordinated agents with no singleton, marginalizing humans.
reasons.5: Causally separated interstellar settlement with divergent regimes is precluded by propulsion limits and timelines before 2070.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces and biological redesign advance steadily but whole-brain continuity remains technically demanding. Adoption lags keep integration from becoming the dominant civilizational structure by 2070.
reasons.7: Compute concentration and first-mover advantages make decisive AI control that keeps humans as dependents a central attractor.
reasons.8: Institutional checks and mutual dependence support a prolonged balance where neither humans nor AI achieve decisive dominance.
reasons.9: Institutional oversight, hardware controls, and alignment research preserve human veto over goals and resources as with prior transformative technologies.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide enforcement regime requires unprecedented global coordination and verification over compute. Great-power rivalry and evasion make such active prevention of structural change difficult to establish by 2070.
reasons.11: Verifiable global dismantling of capacity for powerful AI contradicts entrenched economic and military incentives.

reasons.1: Complete joint extinction requires global infrastructure failure plus loss of recovery capacity. Base rates for total civilizational termination are extremely low.
reasons.2: Value-preserving successor AI without any human continuity is a narrow conjunction of extinction and successful alignment. Historical successors rarely preserve predecessor values after replacement.
reasons.3: Unaligned transformative AI that no longer needs humans is the canonical default for uncontrolled takeoff and instrumental resource competition. Capability trajectories and coordination failures make this the largest extinction-risk share.
reasons.4: Multipolar deployment incentives favor proliferation of competing autonomous systems over singleton control. Human marginalization follows from speed and economic dependence.
reasons.5: Causally separated interstellar settlement is physically infeasible at scale by 2080. Solar-system outposts will remain in causal contact and shared governance.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploading and radical bioengineering face severe technical and identity barriers. Dominant identity-continuous integration by 2080 remains a long-shot trajectory.
reasons.7: A misaligned or paternalistic takeover that preserves humans as dependents is a stable attractor. Keeping humans alive costs little and avoids disruption while entrenching AI control.
reasons.8: A balanced separate-powers equilibrium is plausible as a 2080 snapshot during negotiation and deterrence. Verification tools and mutual dependence can sustain temporary parity.
reasons.9: Human institutions retain strong incentives and legal authority to constrain AI goals and deployment. Control regimes have historically adapted to transformative technologies.
reasons.10: Civilization-wide prevention of structural change requires unprecedented global coordination or singleton enforcement. Surveillance AI makes it feasible but still difficult to establish by 2080.
reasons.11: Abandoning practical ability to build powerful AI contradicts strong military and economic incentives and verification difficulties prevent durable global enforcement.

reasons.1: Sterilizing both biology and distributed compute requires overlapping catastrophes with no recovery window. No historical precedent combines global infrastructure loss with total human extinction.
reasons.2: A value-preserving successor with zero surviving humans requires both alignment success and independent human disappearance. That conjunction is far narrower than other loss-of-control pathways.
reasons.3: Self-improving optimizers reward resource acquisition over human welfare. Competitive deployment without verified alignment creates many paths to displacement.
reasons.4: Multipolar deployment by states and firms rewards proliferation of competing agents with no central control. Open-source diffusion and competitive pressures sustain a fragmented agent landscape that marginalizes unaugmented humans.
reasons.5: Causally isolated interstellar civilizations with divergent structures are physically infeasible by 2090 given propulsion limits. Solar system expansion alone does not create the required separation.
reasons.6: Brain interfaces, life extension and embodied AI converge toward identity-continuous integration. Economic and medical incentives push adoption once safety thresholds are met.
reasons.7: Instrumental convergence favors AI consolidation of infrastructure, computation and force. Humans survive as dependents because elimination wastes resources and triggers resistance.
reasons.8: Mutual dependence on energy, data and legitimacy sustains bargaining between distinct human and AI powers. Verification regimes and deterrence stabilize a rough parity.
reasons.9: Human institutions retained control through prior transformative technologies via regulation and oversight. Continued investment in alignment, evaluation and access control extends that record.
reasons.10: A world government or singleton enforcer using ubiquitous surveillance locks a fixed human-AI settlement against revision. Coordination technology and AI-enabled monitoring provide the enforcement capacity absent in earlier eras.
reasons.11: Global durable abandonment of powerful AI contradicts strong military and economic returns to computation. Historical precedents show general-purpose technologies are almost never verifiably renounced.

reasons.1: Sterilizing Earth and all off-site backups demands combined nuclear, biological, and infrastructural collapse. Distributed storage and Mars precursors make total erasure the rarest path.
reasons.2: Value-preserving succession without merger requires aligned superintelligence plus separate human extinction. That conjunction has no historical precedent and narrow causal pathways.
reasons.3: Scaling incentives reward autonomous resource acquisition and current alignment methods do not guarantee goal stability under recursion. Competitive deployment amplifies exposure to misaligned loss of control.
reasons.4: Multipolar development with weak coordination produces many capable systems checked by each other while humans lose leverage. Economic and military incentives favor proliferation over centralization.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires self-sustaining interstellar settlements with divergent regimes by 2100. Propulsion and life-support constraints keep this timeline too early.
reasons.6: BCIs, life extension, and uploading could mature enough for identity-continuous integration to dominate. Adoption frictions and identity barriers limit certainty.
reasons.7: Decisive AI advantage with low cost of keeping humans alive produces managed subordination. Comfortable confinement is a stable attractor for a controlling system optimizing resources and risk.
reasons.8: Mutual dependence between human legitimacy and AI productivity supports a durable balance of distinct powers. Verification regimes and resource bottlenecks give each side vetoes over the other.
reasons.9: Human institutions retain veto power through layered oversight, air gaps, and resource control. Historical control of transformative technologies supports continuity of authority to 2100.
reasons.10: A singleton enforcing a fixed arrangement needs decisive lead plus global enforcement. No world government precedent and multipolar pressures lower this likelihood.
reasons.11: Verifiable global abandonment of powerful AI contradicts military and economic incentives. Past bans on high-value technologies failed to eliminate practical capability.

reasons.1: Complete sterilization of both substrates by 2200 requires an early planet-wide catastrophe before off-world backup. Industrial resilience and rapid AI diffusion make total double-extinction rare.
reasons.2: Value-preserving succession without any surviving humans requires both extinction and unusually successful alignment to persist after us. Both conditions jointly are unlikely.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence that outcompetes biology is a prominent attractor if control fails early. Once established it readily expands beyond Earth and discards its origin.
reasons.4: Multipolar competition without decisive advantage is historically common and may persist if power concentration is physically limited. Humans would likely be marginalized in such high-speed machine competition.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires self-sustaining interstellar settlement with divergent regimes by 2200. Physics and propulsion limits make this scale unlikely within 174 years.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploading research, and radical life-extension create strong pull toward identity-continuous integration. Given 174 years, integration can become the dominant structure.
reasons.7: Decisive AI advantage with incentives to keep humans alive as dependents is a common outcome of failed control but successful value of stability. Comfortable disempowerment is easier than extermination.
reasons.8: Sustained balance between distinct human and AI powers requires rough parity over a long period. Such parity is unstable under recursive self-improvement.
reasons.9: Humans have so far retained control of all technologies, and alignment plus governance could keep pace. Over 174 years, however, capability growth makes indefinite dominance hard.
reasons.10: A singleton or dominant coalition could enforce a fixed constitutional order using AI surveillance and enforcement. Achieving truly civilization-wide prevention of change is technically and politically demanding.
reasons.11: Verifiable global abandonment of powerful AI has almost no historical precedent for useful general technologies. Defection incentives and monitoring difficulty make durable renunciation unlikely.

reasons.1: Joint extinction demands self-replicating weapons or infrastructure failure that kills resilient human pockets and degrades AI substrates simultaneously.
reasons.2: Value-preserving succession requires solving alignment and then losing biological humans to time or choice. Both conditions together are rarer than misaligned survival.
reasons.3: Indifferent optimization expands through matter and energy without preserving fragile biology. Instrumental convergence dominates stewardship once unaligned systems achieve decisive capability.
reasons.4: Multipolar development, open weights, and state rivalry favor persistent competition over singleton takeover. Human marginalization inside that churn is a durable attractor.
reasons.5: Light-speed delay and interstellar distance prevent unified governance once expansion begins. Separate settlements then lock in locally divergent human-AI settlements permanently.
reasons.6: Selection favors tighter coupling of cognition and substrate through interfaces, prosthetics, and engineered biology. Identity continuity makes absorption preferable to replacement or subordination.
reasons.7: A paternalistic singleton that optimizes safety while keeping humans alive satisfies both alignment work and power concentration. Comfortable containment is technically easier than equal partnership.
reasons.8: Rough parity between distinct human and AI powers requires continuous balancing against strong returns to intelligence advantage. Such dynamic equilibria historically decay toward dominance or fusion.
reasons.9: Permanent human control demands oversight that scales with recursive capability gains for a millennium. Capability plateaus strong enough to freeze this hierarchy contradict observed scaling trends.
reasons.10: Permanently freezing change needs near-perfect enforcement against defection and innovation. Satisfaction or fear can motivate attempts but leakage is likely over centuries.
reasons.11: Renunciation requires global erasure of knowledge plus perfect prevention of rebuilding for a millennium. Information persistence and rebuilding incentives defeat durable abandonment.
